title: This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s
gist: Osmo, a Google Brain spin-out led by Alex Wiltschko, claims its smell foundation model—trained on a proprietary dataset of 10M+ human labels and 800M 'scent tokens'—has reached 'human-level olfactory intelligence' and is already designing commercial fragrances (including for Procter & Gamble). Critics (Avery Gilbert, Michael Schmuker) question undocumented claims, reliance on human panels, and the model's lack of context, while medical diagnostics remains the hard, biggest prize.

insights.claim: Osmo claims its AI model has achieved 'human-level olfactory intelligence', defined as matching an average person at detecting and discriminating smells and a junior perfume designer at creating them.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: A digital olfaction claim of this kind opens new AI modality markets; benchmark verification will determine credibility.

insights.claim: Osmo says that last month its AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world's largest consumer goods companies.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: If replicated, AI scent design threatens the labor model of fragrance houses and could compress fragrance R&D cycles.

insights.claim: Osmo calls its system the world's first foundation model for smell, aiming 'to give computers a sense of smell'.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: Positions Osmo as a platform play rather than a single-application vendor.
insights.quote: “to give computers a sense of smell.”
insights.locator: In a lab near Newark Airport

insights.claim: Alex Wiltschko spun Osmo out of Google Brain in 2023 and applies the standard AI-startup playbook of throwing large amounts of data at hard problems.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: Scale-the-data strategy implies the moat is the proprietary dataset, not the model architecture.
insights.quote: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens.

themes.theme: Proprietary scent data as the moat

insights.claim: Before Osmo, existing databases held fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells, by Wiltschko's count, because chemical sensors are expensive and the fragrance industry is secretive.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: Data scarcity in olfaction makes a large proprietary dataset a meaningful barrier to entry.

insights.claim: Osmo has built its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million 'scent tokens' describing exact molecules and concentrations behind specific odors.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: A 50x jump over prior public smell data; the dataset is the core asset to value.
insights.quote: more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,”

insights.claim: Osmo runs spectrometers and other chemical sensors around the clock and employs about 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas who sniff items and describe them in a standardized fragrance vocabulary; a New Jersey lab has around 30 experienced human sniffers.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: Data generation is labor- and capex-intensive, a cost base to watch and a defensibility factor.
insights.locator: OSMO AI A lot of the

insights.claim: Scent behaves like language: rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter perceived smell, much as word order changes a sentence's meaning, and the scent tokens of a newborn baby overlap massively with those of cooked spaghetti.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: Supports applying language-model techniques to olfaction—a non-obvious transfer of LLM methods to chemistry.
insights.quote: “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,”
insights.locator: Mapping out scents in this way

insights.claim: Osmo operates a school-bus-sized smell-printing robot that mixes ingredients to precise formulas and can design and print scents to order from a ChatGPT-style text prompt, with orders ready in about a week.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: Prompt-to-product manufacturing could shorten fragrance development timelines and enable mass customization.

insights.claim: Osmo's technology has already been used to create retail fragrances, including for Procter & Gamble.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: Large CPG adoption is a commercial validation signal; watch for further brand partnerships and disclosures from P&G.

insights.claim: The Gates Foundation invested $5 million when Osmo launched and later gave a $3.5 million grant to assess insect-repelling molecules, through which Osmo identified eight substances more repellent than DEET.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: Potential disruption of insect-repellent chemistry; a public-health application beyond fragrance.

insights.claim: Osmo has worked with StockX to detect counterfeit sneakers by sensing differences in the chemical composition of shoe materials.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: Olfactory authentication is a new anti-counterfeiting tool for resale marketplaces.

insights.claim: Smell scientist Avery Gilbert argues some of Osmo's marketing claims are undocumented and that its patent filings still rely on human sensory panels and perfumers rather than AI.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: Gap between AI marketing and patented methods is a diligence red flag for investors.
insights.quote: “This heavy reliance on human sensory judgments seems odd for a company premised on super-cool AI,”

insights.claim: Michael Schmuker, a former Osmo consultant, calls the technology an achievement and co-created an open-source, reverse-engineered version of Osmo's 2023 model, though it lacks the data Osmo has since collected.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: Model architecture is replicable; Osmo's defensibility rests on its accumulated data.

insights.claim: Schmuker warns that smell models may miss context: Camembert shares a molecule with used nappies, and humans distinguish them only through context, which matters little in a fragrance lab but could limit Osmo's use as an 'olfactive channel' for AI world models.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: Context-dependence limits expansion beyond controlled fragrance settings into real-world sensing.
insights.quote: Context is very important for smell. The same molecule may evoke a different association depending on context,

insights.claim: Wiltschko envisions Osmo's technology eventually being used for threat detection at airports and for diagnosing diseases.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: Security and medical sensing are large TAMs but distant; treat as option value.

insights.claim: Medical diagnostics via smell, such as detecting tumors as dogs have in pilot studies, is the biggest prize but requires much better sensor technology and continued model improvement.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: Progress in chemical sensor hardware is the gating factor to watch for diagnostic applications.
insights.quote: Medical diagnostics is the biggest prize.

insights.claim: Osmo deliberately avoids attacking medical diagnostics head-on, citing a history of expensive failures, and instead builds a broad foundation 'at the foothills' while sending exploratory projects toward harder applications.
insights.speaker: Amit Katwala
insights.so_what: A revenue-first, platform-then-verticals strategy reduces burn risk relative to diagnostics-first olfaction startups.
insights.quote: So what we’re doing is building this foundation at the foothills of all these mountains.
